content.thinking:
I need to plan the file carefully in one pass, making sure the SDK requirements are met—specifically that there's exactly one root joint and that parts without explicit joints resolve safely, since the structure deals with mostly static objects and only a few moving parts.

So I'm sketching helper functions for boxes, cylinders, and rods, plus an extruded island base shape. I'm working out the geometry math for the extrusion thickness direction and making sure the base sits properly on the floor at y=0, accounting for the overall height scale of the scene.

Now I'm setting the scale references: palms around 1.4m, tents 0.6m, camels 0.45m, and laying out the composition with the red tent to the viewer's left, blue tent right, pool centered at back, and palms behind.

For the pool, I'm using a low-poly cylinder for the water with a darker sand collar ring to suggest a sunken basin, plus a stacked rock formation behind it feeding a light-blue waterfall strip into the water. Camels go front-right standing and front-left sitting, with a fire tripod nearby, and three palm trees positioned behind the scene.

For the palms, I'm sweeping tapered trunks with bark ring striping, then building fronds from leaf-outline extrusions oriented along angled directions with a drooping tip segment attached to each base frond for a natural curve.

I should add a thin midrib rod for the frond for a cheap detail boost. For the trunk, I'm thinking through the catmull-rom curve with a tapering radius swept along a heptagon section, but I realize skinning this to bones is risky since vertices might snap to the nearest joint by proximity, which could wrongly bind trunk geometry to a tent hinge joint rather than the root -- I need to guard against that.

Setting bone assignments explicitly...

Now I'm working out the camel geometry: building the body as a loft/sweep with yaw rotation to orient it facing a given direction, defining local coordinates for body stations running from rump to chest with varying width and height to form the hump silhouette.

I'm shaping the single dromedary hump as a squashed sphere positioned on the back under where the saddle would sit, then starting the neck as a smooth catmull-rom curve sweeping upward and forward with a tapering radius.

Still building the camel head...

Hind legs get similar hip-to-hock-to-foot joint coordinates, plus flat cylinder foot pads and a rod tail. I'm settling on tan camel coloring with a lighter belly, pale muzzle, and dark hooves, using countershading on the body loft. For the sitting pose, I'll reuse the same build function with a `sit` parameter that lowers the body and tucks the legs into lying capsule shapes.

Now I'm defining the folded leg geometry for the sitting pose and the neck curve rising from chest to head, then sketching how to approximate a draped saddle blanket using angled planes instead of a flat box.

Adding more blanket geometry...

Then I plan to add small cones as tassels along the bottom edge in blue and red, plus saddlebag boxes.

For the bedroll, I'm working out the rotated cylinder orientation across the body, combining a z-axis rotation with yaw so the cylinder's axis correctly points along the horse's x direction, double-checking how three.js composes the Euler XYZ rotation order to get the right world-frame result.

Now I'm designing the tents, starting with the red tent on the left: a bedouin-style ridge pole tent with sloped roof panels, gable triangles at front and back, a scalloped valance with diamond trim, and poles with gold finials, setting local dimensions for width, depth, wall height, and ridge height.

I'll combine yaw and local rotation using Euler order [0, yaw, rz] so the tent's overall orientation composes correctly with the roof slope rotation. For decoration, I'm adding a thin trimmed valance band along the front gable edges—small boxes positioned along the slope with a diamond-pattern texture, offset slightly forward from the roof surface.

Now I'm building the front gable structure: a closed back wall extruded from the pentagon/triangle outline, and an open front with a dark interior visible through two hinged curtain flaps (cream-colored boxes with joint bones at their outer edges) that sweep open like tied-back drapes. The side walls are thin fabric-colored boxes spanning the tent's depth, with the roof overlapping them, and the back wall left plain and solid.

For the interior, I'm adding cushion boxes, a textured carpet, and a chest -- plus a carpet outside the entrance on the sand, using a thin box geometry (rather than a plane, to avoid rotation-order headaches with combining tilt and yaw) so I can texture all its faces and simply yaw it in place. I'm also planning front corner support poles with finials, angled outward as guy poles anchoring the tent to the ground.

I'm designing slanted outer poles with gold sphere finials, plus thin guy ropes running from the ridge tips down to ground stakes, and a vertical ridge post with a gold sphere topper. Since there are two tents in different colors, I'll write a reusable `tent(cx, cz, yaw, main, trim, accent)` function with a local coordinate helper that rotates points by yaw, so I don't have to duplicate geometry for each tent. For rocks, I'm using low-detail icosahedron/dodecahedron geometries, flattened, scaled, and rotated, with grayish tones.

Now I'm adding a rock-placement helper that sets height based on ground level and radius, then moving on to desert vegetation -- spiky agave clusters and dry grass tufts built from thin cone "spikes" radiating outward from a base point, using a bone/sides option to control blade shape. I'm skipping grass card sprites and starting the campfire setup next.

For the campfire, I'm planning a ring of small rocks, a tripod of dark rods, a hanging hemisphere cauldron, and glowing orange flame cones using a glow kit, plus small glowing lantern boxes on the tents. I'm also sketching out a lathe-generated pot profile with a curved neck for clay jars, alongside simpler props like stools, woven baskets, crates, and water jugs.

I'm working out a closed, non-self-intersecting outline for the pot shape, then planning to paint horizontal stripe bands by height using the lathe segment coordinates to distinguish trim color from clay color. For the water pool, I'm considering a turquoise lathe disc with a lighter inner ring for visual depth.

Now I'm making the water pool elliptical by scaling it, sitting the water disc slightly above the sand ground with a darker wet-sand rim disc just beneath it, surrounded by rocks. I'm adding a thin waterfall box in light cyan cascading down the back rocks, foam spheres at its base, and a larger rock stack further back for depth, while also planning subtle ripple rings on the water surface using thin flat lathe shapes.

Now I'm defining the base diorama outline as an irregular low-poly blob roughly 2.6 units wide, generating points around a circle with varied radii so it reads as chunky and faceted rather than smooth, keeping it star-shaped but non-intersecting, then planning sand mottling paint across the extruded top face.

Writing paint and slab logic...

Checking palm height fits within scale (~1.5 total, bottom at y=0), then adding a few thin dark ellipsoids for sand ripples near the dunes. Setting trunk height to around 1.05.

Writing palm tree generator function...

Still working out frond geometry...

Still defining leaf outline points...

Still shaping the outline profile...

Now I'm estimating total part counts: 11 fronds per palm across 3 palms, plus tents, camels, rocks, and agave plants could push the scene toward 700-850 parts, risky against a 1000 budget. I should cut back—dropping midrib rods, reducing fronds to 9 per palm, and trimming agave blade counts to stay safely under the limit.

Now I'm setting up a shared color palette with sand, rock, water, and foam tones to keep the flat-color count under 40.

Still defining the palette...

Now I'm planning the SVG texture generator functions—patterns for blankets, carpets, and trim strips using diamond motifs in the red/blue/cream palette, built as reusable string-producing functions.

I'm figuring out how these textures map onto the tent's box geometry: since each box face shows the full texture stretched to its own aspect ratio, I need to size the viewBox for each piece (trim strip, carpet top, blanket sides) so the pattern doesn't look distorted on the visible faces, while accepting some stretching on faces that won't be seen.

For coloring, I'll pass a tint of white for the colored fabric textures and consider adding subtle position-based stripes along the x-axis on the roof boxes using the 3D coordinates rather than UV mapping.

I'll type the color helper as string or Paint, importing Paint as a type-only import since it's exported as a class. Now I'm setting up the imports and starting the file structure, pulling in THREE, the builder, and outline point types.

I'm bringing in rng for randomness, catmull for path smoothing, and several paint utilities like countershade, mottle, stripes, plus svg texture and glow kit helpers. With the meta object and Fillc type defined, I'm starting the build function by creating a builder named "desertOasis" with a base joint at the origin, then setting up a seeded random generator and a helper for placing geometry with color and position.

Defining shorthand functions...

Writing yaw rotation helper...

I'm confirming the Euler rotation order applies Z first, then generating the island outline shape using a noisy radius function, mapping the 2D outline points into world x/z coordinates.

Now I'm extruding the base shape upward by a thin thickness, verifying the normal direction works out to point along y so the ground surface is correctly oriented, and setting up striped sand coloring along the strata layers.

Checking the overall footprint, the extents are running slightly too large, so I'm scaling the tent positions and sizes down to fit within a roughly 2.7 by 2.4 meter area, then working out the rotation math for the red tent so its yaw angle correctly orients its front face.

I'm placing the red tent toward the left and the blue tent toward the right with opposite facing angles to mirror the reference layout, then adjusting the pool's position and radius to avoid overlapping the tent corners.

Now I'm positioning the two camels: the standing one angled to face slightly away, and the sitting one rotated toward the right to match the reference pose, along with figuring out where the tripod fire sits relative to the sitting camel.

Checking the blue tent placement against the camel footprint, I'm worried about overlap near z -0.25, so I'm adjusting positions—moving the camel to (0.8,0.38) and the tent to (0.72,-0.3)—then re-verifying the ellipse bounds to confirm everything stays within the scene boundary.

I decide to enlarge the tent base dimensions so it reads as roughly 1.5-3 meters across, settling on rx around 1.4 and rz 1.2 for a believable size. Then I move on to placing boulders in the front-left area and positioning palm trees behind the pool around z -0.75 with a height near 1.15.

I continue scattering the palms with slight lean variations and varying heights for naturalism, then check the rock placements near the waterfall's back wall around z -0.55. With the environment set, I start writing the tent-building function with parameters for position, yaw, fabric colors, and texture inputs.

Writing tent geometry code...

Still placing walls...

Now I'm adding front curtain flaps covering the left and right sides with hinge joints, giving them cream fabric color and attaching them via bone-based boxes at the gable edges.

I'm also adding a decorative trim band along the front roof edges, positioning it on the slanted roof surface with proper rotation and texture to simulate a lintel valance.

Now I'm adding ridge poles with gold finial spheres at the apex, placing vertical rods at the front and back of the roof peak for decoration.

I'm also laying out the outer slanted support poles at the four corners with gold spheres on top, then adding guy ropes running from the ridge finial and corner poles down to ground stakes, plus small tassels hanging beneath the finial for ornamental detail.

Now I'm shifting to the interior: placing a floor rug with a textured pattern, scattered cushions nearby, and a small wooden chest with dark decorative bands and a gold lock latch.

Writing camel function body...

I'm realizing there's an orientation issue: the loft's width/height axes default to world-X alignment, but when the body is yawed the tube direction rotates away from that, so I need to reassign width/height relative to the yawed binormal rather than assuming world-X.

For the hump shape, I'm applying a non-uniform local scale (stretched along z and y) before the yaw rotation, since scale happens in local space prior to the rotation transform being applied.

Now I'm working out the neck and head geometry: defining a curved path of points from chest to neck tip for both standing and sitting poses, then placing the skull and snout capsules at the neck's end, angling the head forward and downward the way a camel naturally tilts it.

Positioning the smaller facial features next -- the lower jaw, nose pad, eyes, and ears -- then adding a halter made from a thin torus wrapped around the snout, colored with the accent tone.

I'm also adding strap rods connecting the halter to behind the ears, plus a drooping lead rope rendered as a smooth sweep from the chin down to near the ground.

For the standing legs, I'm sweeping polylines through hip, knee, and foot points with tapered radii, using the coat color with a darker callus patch at the knee and a cylindrical foot pad at the base.

For the hind legs I'm working out camel-specific joint geometry where the thigh angles forward-down and the hock angles back, placing hip, stifle, and hock points with careful y-coordinates so the hock sits higher and further back than a standard leg before dropping to the foot near ground level.

Now I'm switching to the sitting pose, defining tucked front and hind legs as folded segments with points for hip/elbow/forefoot and hip/hock/foot respectively, using varying radii to taper each limb toward the foot.

Then I'm adjusting the body position lower to sit on the folded legs, adding a curved tail sweep with a dark tuft sphere at the tip, and starting the saddle blanket as a flat box positioned over the camel's hump.

Actually, I'm reconsidering the blanket shape—using hanging side panels on either side of the body instead of a top-only piece, plus a wider top box to drape over the hump area, both textured with a blanket pattern.

For saddlebags, I'm adding brown leather boxes hanging outside the blanket on each side, with strap rods connecting them. I'm also placing a bedroll cylinder over the hump, rotated so its axis runs crosswise along the body after applying the yaw transform.

Adding rolled-end bands and tassels...

I'm deciding to skip chest calluses and mane tufts, but adding a small beard spike below the chin and tiny dark nostril spheres for extra detail.

Writing palm generator function...

Adding a crown sphere and base flare cone to the trunk, then setting up palm fronds with randomized yaw, elevation, and droop angles for a natural asymmetric look.

Still defining frond profile logic...

Checking that the lower edge points stay distinct from the upper ones at the boundaries so the zigzag doesn't self-intersect, then verifying the segment length scaling works correctly when splitting into two segments with an offset.

For the date clusters, I'm planning two clusters per palm with spheres arranged around a circle, roughly 36 total sphere parts across three palms, and deciding to merge them into one geometry per palm using mergeGeometries since they share color and bone.

Now I'm designing the agave plant function, generating spikes radiating outward from a center point with alternating colors and tilted directions for a more natural splayed look.

Then I'm adding a dry grass tuft with thin outward spikes, and a rock generator using dodecahedron geometry with randomized scale and rotation plus a mottled, countershaded paint for natural coloring variation.

Now I'm setting up the pool with a wet sand rim ring and a water cylinder nested inside, positioned slightly above the sand so the water surface sits just higher than the rim.

For depth I'm adding a darker water disc toward the middle plus ripple rings, then placing a ring of small rocks around the pool edge, leaving a gap at the back for the waterfall and stacking larger cliff rocks there.

Now I'm positioning the waterfall itself: a thin tilted water strip with foam streak accents and a foam cluster at the base, checking that its z-position sits just in front of the cliff rocks so it reads as falling off them, and confirming the pool's wet rim overlaps the cliff base for continuity.

I'm also checking tent placement against the pool so they don't overlap—spacing the red and other tent further out at roughly ±0.88 on x to clear the pool's footprint, while keeping the camel and leaning palm crowns positioned naturally around the scene.

For props, I'm building jar pots using a lathe profile with painted clay bands, then chests made from boxes with lids, bands, and corner locks, stacking a couple near the tents in a wood brown tone.

Alongside those, I'm adding a stool from a box top with rod legs, a woven basket cylinder with striped grain texture and a torus rim, and a fire pit with dark dodecahedron stones ringed around glowing flame cones.

I'm setting up a tripod with three rods meeting at an apex above the fire, hanging a sphere cauldron from a chain-like rod sweep, plus water jars by the tents and a cluster of merged pebble rocks for scattered ground detail.

For the dune edges I'm placing a few flattened, light-colored sand spheres low to the ground so they don't poke through the base, then adding subtle ripple marks using tiny rotated boxes merged into a single dark-sand part.

Now I'm setting up the tent skeleton with five joints—four flap hinges plus a root—using downward-facing hinge directions for the curtain pivots, then moving on to generate SVG texture patterns for the fabric.

Writing SVG pattern code...

Adding inner field and lozenge details to the rug design. I'm verifying the gable extrude math checks out with the tent's yaw rotation and local coordinate axes, then moving on to constructing the interior walls and front opening below the gable.

Now I'm defining the full tent function signature with parameters for colors, textures, and furnishings, then tallying up the detail elements per tent — roof pieces, bands, walls, poles, ropes, rug, cushions, chest, lantern — landing around fifty details total. I'm starting on the gold finial sphere next.

Still placing corner poles and guy ropes with stakes...

I'm checking type correctness for the part parameters—making sure coordinate arrays, rotations, and scale values match the expected number/array types, and confirming the needed options interfaces are properly imported. I'm also trimming an unused color parameter before sketching out the camel's standing pose with head and neck positioned relative to the body.

Now I'm adjusting the sitting variant's neck height and double-checking that all imported utilities and helper functions get used so nothing triggers unused-variable errors. With that confirmed, I'm moving into the palm tree code—placing the crown ball and generating nine fronds with varied yaw angles and upright/drooping orientations.

Writing frond and date geometry...

Working out the lantern cord and glowing box details hanging from the tent ridge, then moving on to define a reusable chest function with a wood-paneled body and fixed proportions.

Adding lid bands, lock hardware, and grain texture...
